articles.title: Trump announces new trade tariffs: Which countries are affected?
articles.summary: The US is planning tariffs on 14 economies it accuses of using subsidies to help their industries overproduce.
articles.body:
The Trump administration has announced plans to impose new trade tariffs on 14 of its major trading partners, including China, the European Union and India, accusing them of flooding world markets with cheap goods. China faces the highest rates.

The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the duties on Wednesday following an eight-month investigation into what Washington calls “structural excess capacity”.

A senior US official told Reuters that USTR defines this as countries “promoting production and capacity divorced from the realities of demand and market principles”, including through subsidies and other industrial policies.

The tariffs are the latest attempt to rebuild Trump’s sweeping import taxes that the US Supreme Court struck down in February.

The latest tariffs are being imposed under Section 301, part of a 1974 US trade law, which allows Washington to penalise countries it determines are treating US businesses unfairly. Trump used it to place large tariffs on Chinese goods during his first term, and those tariffs survived challenges in court.

The new tariffs are Trump’s latest attempt to bring back the “ Liberation Day ” tariffs he announced in April 2025 shortly after he began his second term in the White House. He imposed those under an emergency powers law but, in February this year, the Supreme Court ruled that the law did not allow him to impose trade tariffs.

“It’s supposed to be for international economic emergencies,” Dmitry Grozoubinski, a trade policy expert, said of the emergency law. “Tariffs are like taxes. You can’t really fight emergencies with mild taxes.”

The administration then used another law to put temporary 10 percent tariffs on trading partners in place, which ran out in July. It then replaced those with tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on 60 economies, which together supply almost everything the US imports. This time it used Section 301, arguing that those countries do not do enough to keep out goods made with forced labour.

Grozoubinski said Section 301 was designed to allow a president to hit back quickly at one country over one industry, not to tax almost every import. “The legislation is supposed to be a scalpel, and they used it like a flamethrower,” he said. “It is not meant to set the US tariff code, which is what this effectively did.”

The recent investigation into the “structural excess capacity” of trading partners began in March and covered industries from steel and cars to computer chips and solar panels. It examined government subsidies, wages suppressed by the state and the operations of state-owned companies.

Washington argues that this support enables foreign factories to sell their goods more cheaply around the world, undercutting American manufacturers and discouraging investment in the US. The senior official told Reuters that the new duties would not be added on top of the forced labour tariffs.

The investigation covered 16 economies, and tariffs have been proposed for 14 of them: China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. For now, Mexico and Norway, which were also investigated, have been spared.

The Trump administration views China as the biggest offender, pointing to its steel, aluminium, electric cars, household appliances and solar panels industries. Beijing rejects the accusation and says its exports are simply competitive. Washington also accuses Chinese companies of investing in Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia to bypass earlier US tariffs.

For the other economies, Washington pointed to the large trade surpluses of Germany and Ireland as evidence against the EU. It also singled out the car industries of China and Japan, Singapore’s computer chips and Norway’s fuel and seafood exports for criticism.

The senior official cited by Reuters did not provide rates for most countries ahead of their publication in the Federal Register. However, China will face the highest charges. The official said its proposed 20 percent excess capacity tariff would come on top of the roughly 25 percent in tariffs set during Trump’s first term. That keeps China above Vietnam, which also faces a proposed rate of 20 percent.

The official said the new duties would not break the tariff limits in trade deals the Trump administration has negotiated. According to earlier Reuters reporting, those include caps of 15 percent for the EU, Japan and South Korea, and 19 percent for Malaysia.

For China, the limit is 20 percent on tariffs imposed during Trump’s second term, under a trade truce with Beijing that expires on January 10.

India has no signed trade deal with the US. The two sides agreed the outline of one in February, but it was never finalised, and talks have dragged on for months. On November 14, Indian foreign minister S Jaishankar said a deal could be sealed soon.

Grozoubinski said the timing is significant. The proposal comes just weeks after midterm elections in which Trump’s Republican Party suffered unprecedented electoral losses, in which the cost of living and trade tariffs were major issues. A Reuters/Ipsos poll after the vote indicated that 62 percent of respondents would support efforts to scrap trade tariffs.

“One interpretation is, like, OK, they’re going to chill out on these tariffs, because basically every time they say the word tariffs, people remember that their costs are really high and get angrier,” Grozoubinski said. “This shows that at least on some level, they are still prepared despite the headwinds, to go ahead and push that button.”

Hisham Wahby, an independent political analyst, said the key question after the vote was whether Trump would “double down or pull back”. Days after the midterms, Trump named his longtime adviser, the hardline anti-immigration activist Stephen Miller, as White House chief of staff. Wahby said that “was a clear indicator he is going to double down”.

US importers are currently challenging the forced labour tariffs at the US Court of International Trade, and Grozoubinski called the reasoning behind them “incredibly dubious”. Accusations about subsidies, he said, will be easier to defend.

“One theory is maybe they’re going to impose these little tariffs now, but if their big tariffs on everybody on forced labour get cancelled, they can fall back and say, we’ve already done the investigation,” he said. In that case, he added, the new tariffs would “replace the tariffs that replaced the tariffs that replaced the tariffs that replaced the Liberation Day tariffs”.

The announcement also comes weeks before the US-China trade truce, agreed between President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jingping last year, runs out, while trade talks with India remain unfinished.

Wahby said the decision is hard to explain in economic terms. “He lost the midterms because of the cost of living, because of the price of goods. Small businesses were suffering,” he said. “Households are suffering, small businesses are suffering, and you double down on it.”

Grozoubinski said the new tariffs will certainly be challenged in court. However, he said they were likely to stay in place while the cases went on, because lower court rulings are usually appealed and put on hold. The emergency tariffs, he noted, stayed in force for months after the trade court first ruled against them, until the Supreme Court struck them down.

He added that these latest tariffs stand a better chance of surviving than earlier ones, because foreign subsidies are a more believable complaint than forced labour.

“There’s probably something there,” he said. If the investigation genuinely found unfair practices, he said, the Supreme Court may decide that Trump is within his rights and that it is up to Congress to stop him.

“Of the tariffs he has imposed so far, these, at least from the outside and without having any of the details, are probably the most legally robust,” he said.

Will Trump’s tariffs restore manufacturing in the US?

The Trump administration argues that tariffs will push companies to build factories in the US to avoid paying import duties.

Grozoubinski said tariffs could help American companies that compete with imports, but will hurt those that rely on them. A US carmaker gains when foreign cars cost more, he said, but loses when the imported steel, engines and parts it needs also cost more.

The bigger problem, he said, is that nobody knows how long the tariffs will last. A new factory can take a decade or more to pay for itself, while Trump raises and lowers tariffs as negotiations shift. Congress could also limit his power to impose them, and a future president could scrap them altogether.

A company weighing a new US factory would worry about that, he said: “I can’t guarantee those tariffs will still be around for all the 10 years I need them.”

“If I wanted to use the US tariff code to encourage people to build factories in the US, I would not do it this way,” he said.

The most immediate cost is likely to fall on US companies and households that depend on imports. “If you make components from somewhere else more expensive, then, really simplistically, the people who buy them in your country lose out, and the people who make them in your country win,” Grozoubinski said.

Wahby said small businesses would be among the hardest hit. “How is that going to increase jobs if small businesses can’t manage to buy what they need from China?” he asked.

Markets were already uneasy, and US stocks came under pressure on Tuesday as reports of the plan emerged.

Abroad, the tariffs risk straining the US-China truce, which expires in January, and could complicate trade talks with India. They are also likely to anger US allies who already accuse Washington of breaching existing trade agreements. “This is not a free market economy when you’re putting tariffs on everybody,” Wahby said.

At home, the move sets up a clash with Democrats, who take control of both chambers of Congress in January. Wahby said they would push back, but their power is limited because Trump can veto legislation. “They will stand up to him, but we don’t know how effectively,” he said.

articles.title: Reality TV's Georgia Harrison backs extending sex education to 18
articles.summary: Georgia Harrison, who was a victim of "revenge porn", says children are exposed to online "poison".
articles.body:
TV celebrity and "revenge porn" victim Georgia Harrison has urged MPs to back a new law that would extend compulsory relationships and sex education (RSE) up to the age of 18.

The Only Way Is Essex and Love Island star led a protest outside Parliament to call for the change, telling the BBC it was needed to combat the "poison" young people were being exposed to online.

The demonstration comes ahead of a debate and vote next week on a draft law that would legally require all further education providers in England to teach RSE to under-18s.

The Department for Education (DfE) said it was exploring how RSE could be extended to colleges.

Compulsory relationships and sex education currently stops at age 16 in England, meaning sixth forms and colleges are not required to teach the subject.

Speaking in Westminster, Harrison said: "Between 16 and 18 is the age that people first start having sex.

"It doesn't make sense that we're abandoning them at that time."

Harrison said "misogynists" had "sold our young people advice, but really, it's poison".

"We need to undo it and the only way to undo it is through education," Harrison said.

Harrison was a victim of so-called revenge porn . Fellow reality TV performer Stephen Bear was jailed for posting intimate footage of the pair online, which he had filmed at his home in Loughton in Essex.

She said making RSE mandatory to age 18 could help prevent intimate image abuse of the kind she suffered.

The campaign outside Parliament was organised by media organisation LADbible.

The Relationships and Sex Education (Further Education Sector) Bill has been put forward by Alistair Strathern, the Labour MP for the Hitchin constituency in Bedfordshire and Hertfordshire.

It is a private members' bill, which are only debated on Fridays and rarely become law.

However, Strathern told the BBC he had "a good chance of making real change".

"I've been really encouraged by the response we've got from ministers so far," he said.

A DfE spokesperson said: "Supporting children and young people to grow up happy and healthy whilst safeguarding them from harm on and offline is a job for us all.

"We're determined that across our education system, schools and colleges play their part.

"That's why we have rolled out mandatory RHSE [relationships, sex and health education] in schools and we are exploring how we can extend this to colleges too."

The bill follows a petition by the survivor-led campaign group Make it Mandatory, which called for sex education to be mandated to 18.

Faustine Petron said she founded the campaign after surviving a coercive and abusive relationship when she was under 18.

"I thought back to the lack of education I had about the signs of abusive behaviour, grooming and coercive control," Petron said.

"I was shocked in my research to find out that sex education ends at 16. I thought 'how nonsensical'.

"I got into the relationship at 16. Why stop and have this dangerous loophole in the law?"

articles.title: Martha Ford, former Lions owner with link to auto giants, dies at 101
articles.summary: Martha Firestone Ford, the tire heiress who became a link between two of the automotive industry’s most iconic families and later took over the NFL’s Detroit Lions, has died.
articles.body: Martha Firestone Ford, the tire heiress who became a link between two of the automotive industry’s most iconic families and later took over the NFL’s Detroit Lions, has died. She was 101. The Lions say she died Tuesday at her home in Grosse Pointe, Michigan, surrounded by family. No cause of death was given. Ford was a granddaughter of tire magnate Harvey Firestone, and her husband, William Clay Ford Sr., was Henry Ford’s grandson. He also owned the Lions for a half-century before his death in 2014. Martha Ford then took over his controlling interest in the team, keeping it within the family. Although she seldom spoke to reporters or commented publicly on the direction of the franchise, her influence was felt. She was in charge of the team from 2014 until 2020, when she turned the Lions over to her daughter, Sheila Ford Hamp. The Lions made the playoffs in 2014, but lost seven of their first eight games the following season. In November 2015, the team fired its president and general manager in a midseason shakeup. When she announced the changes, Ford told fans the franchise intended to “identify and hire the very best leadership in order to produce a consistently, winning football team.” The Lions played better down the stretch that season, and after hiring Bob Quinn as their new general manager, they returned to the playoffs a year later. “Martha was special,” NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said in a statement. “She cared so deeply about her family, the players, their fans, and the city of Detroit. She was committed to making the Lions - and the game of football - better. Martha and her husband, William Clay Ford, led the franchise with dignity and integrity. We will miss her kindness and sweet sense of humor. We extend our deepest condolences to her children, the entire Ford family, and the Lions’ organization.” Born Sept. 16, 1925, in Akron, Ohio, Martha Parke Firestone graduated from Vassar College in 1946 and married William Clay Ford the next year. Their wedding received a huge amount of coverage - looking back in 2014, the Akron Beacon Journal described it as “Akron’s royal wedding” - and the marriage joined two families that already had a long history. Harvey Firestone, the founder of the Firestone Tire and Rubber Co., was a close friend of Ford Motor Co. founder Henry Ford. Ford chose Firestone to supply the tires for the first Model T in 1906. The two men often went on long camping trips together, sometimes accompanied by their friend Thomas Edison. Martha and William Clay Ford had three daughters and a son. Their son, William Clay Ford Jr., is the current executive chairman of Ford Motor Co. In 2001, Bridgestone/Firestone and Ford severed their nearly 100-year relationship because of a dispute over a series of deadly tire failures on the Ford Explorer. Sheila Ford Hamp is the Lions’ principal owner and chairman. William Clay Ford’s first full season leading the Lions was in 1964, seven years after they won an NFL title. Since that 1957 championship, the franchise has won playoff games in 1992 and 2023 and has not played in the Super Bowl. Although Martha Ford kept a low profile, the shakeup in the middle of the 2015 season was a sign that she was more than willing to bring about change in an effort to reverse the team’s fortunes. Then-coach Jim Caldwell said she was very much a presence within the organization. “I think visible ownership is great, and Mrs. Ford does it extremely well,” Caldwell said in 2015. “She’s there before games and she’s there after games, and I think guys enjoy that part of it. She comes to practice and things of that nature, so it’s been fun.” Even at 101, she attended games, including a win over the Minnesota Vikings earlier this month. Martha Ford also made an impact in the Detroit community. She was an officer on the board for Detroit Lions Charities and on the board of the Henry Ford Health System. Martha and William Clay Ford were credited with helping establish the Maplegrove Center, a substance abuse treatment facility in West Bloomfield. In 2017, Forbes estimated Martha Ford’s net worth at more than $1.4 billion. She is survived by her four children, 14 grandchildren, and 17 great-grandchildren. ___ See AP’s full NFL coverage here

articles.title: A rising star in China is the latest victim of Xi’s purge
articles.summary: He was on the rise among China’s political elite, hosting tech leaders and senior American officials.
articles.body: He was on the rise among China’s political elite, hosting tech leaders and senior American officials. But now Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s influential politburo, appears to be the latest senior official brought down by President Xi Jinping’s sweeping purge. The hammer unexpectedly came down on Chen in the form of a two-line bulletin on the Xinhua news agency Tuesday: He is “suspected of serious violations of Party discipline and law and is currently under disciplinary review and supervisory investigation” — a common euphemism for corruption crackdowns on ruling Communist Party officials under Xi. Public announcements such as these usually mark the end of a political career in China. Chen has made no public statement. He is the fourth politburo member to be purged in less than two years, part of a broader crackdown that has swept aside top military leaders as Xi consolidates power. He is set to extend his rule next year, at a party congress that is held once every five years and looms over the preceding months. But Chen’s abrupt downfall took many close observers of China by surprise, given his profile and career path would usually point to a bright future. “He was potentially going to the highest level, which would be the standing committee. And I think from a lot of Western observers, people thought he had even better prospects,” Damien Ma, the Singapore-based director of the Carnegie China think tank, told NBC News. Xi’s pursuit of loyalty Some analysts have speculated that Xi, increasingly viewed as likely to rule for life, may have been purging a viable replacement. Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London, said however that Chen was “someone who could rise further but not as a successor.” Chen, a 62-year-old technocrat known as a friend of foreign business and an advocate for AI, was an environmental scientist who studied in London and swiftly rose through the party’s ranks. He served as China’s environmental minister, Beijing’s mayor and the party secretary in Shanghai — a post once held by Xi and widely considered a stepping stone to bigger things. Just last month, Chen hosted Apple Chairman Tim Cook, welcoming the U.S. tech giant to “make full use of Shanghai’s strengths” and bring more products to the city, a financial and cultural hub that has long served as a connection between China and the international community. In his last public appearance last week, during a tour of a shipping facility, Chen called for advancing the industry’s digital transformation. By Wednesday, Chen’s name has been removed from some official websites. A webpage on the Shanghai government site showing that meeting with Cook is now showing a 404 message, or not found. Chen is just the latest senior official in the crosshairs of Xi’s long-running anti-corruption campaign and emphasis on party discipline, which analysts say is as much about loyalty as it is about reform. “It is a warning to all technocrats, as Chen was a rising star among technocrats and had no apparent failures in a technocratic way. So, message is: adhere to strict party discipline and demonstrate unquestionable loyalty to Xi or else,” Tsang said. The party’s Central Committee, which has about 200 mostly male leaders, vowed to “ensure more rigorous discipline enforcement, and make full use of discipline as a guide, restraint, guarantee, and incentive” at its closed-door gathering, the fifth plenum, last month. “What they’ve been building as part of this discipline machine over the last 15 years is to kind of implement their sort of internal operating system of how they deal with, let’s say, bad eggs within the party,” Ma, of Carnegie China, said. “The top leadership is normalizing this anti-corruption, this self-cleansing,” Ma said. “It is now a normal part of what the party expects, and they’re trying to embed that over time and down to every single level,” he added. The Chinese government has not announced any charges against Chen, who was the youngest member of the country’s elite decision-making body. The 24-member Politburo was unveiled in 2022 but is now down to 21 members after the purges. Last month, top general Zhang Shengmin was elevated to the body in a rare addition. Chen’s undoing comes a year before the party’s top leadership is reshuffled at the 21st Communist Party Congress, when Xi is expected to solidify control even further and cement another five-year term at the helm of the country. From London to Shanghai Born in 1964, Chen studied at the prestigious Tsinghua university, long a major pipeline for senior party officials and where he served as president from 2012 to 2015. His name has now been removed from Tsinghua’s online list of former presidents. After studying at Tsinghua in the 1980s, he moved for a decade to Britain, where he obtained a doctorate from Imperial College London in 1993. Chen returned to Tsinghua’s environmental science and engineering department in 1998 before being named the university’s president in 2012, according to an official biography. He’s authored dozens of papers, including on carbon emission reduction and water quality monitoring. The relatively young Chen would ride around campus on his bike and built a reputation for pushing institutional reforms in his three years at the helm of the university, according to an article in People’s Digest, a magazine affiliated with the People’s Daily, the community party’s official newspaper. The article, titled “From University President to Cabinet Minister,” was published in 2015, the same year he was picked to lead the Environmental Protection Ministry. In 2017, Chen became mayor of the capital, Beijing, where he oversaw the 2022 Winter Olympics during the Covid pandemic. Later that year he was transferred to Shanghai and became the party chief, a coveted role that Xi took on himself in 2007 before becoming the country’s leader in 2013. There, he became heavily involved with the tech industry, regularly hosting CEOs and advocating for more investment into Shanghai, where the World AI Conference was hosted earlier this year. Chen hosted Elon Musk in 2023 to discuss Tesla’s operations in the city. Last year, he accompanied Xi to an AI hub there. And last month, Chen met with several European tech leaders, in addition to hosting Cook. Alongside the top post in Shanghai, Chen also was elected for a five-year term as a member of the Politburo, China’s elite decision-making body headed by Xi. While the Politburo is not the absolute apex of power, he was seen as a contender the much-smaller Politburo’s Standing Committee, which is made up of the country’s highest ranking officials. “If you’re party secretary of one of the four big municipalities, Beijing, Shanghai, Chongqing and Tianjin, you have pretty good prospects. That’s sort of an indication that you’re on your way up,” Ma said. Whether or not Chen’s ousting deals a blow to the country’s technology ambitions and its race for dominance in artificial intelligence, remains to be seen, Ma said. But either way, his downfall will force a rethink among those seeking to predict the route to power in modern China. “Part of it is thinking through what is really the new criteria to get to the top, and they may not be what we thought just a few months ago,” Ma added.

articles.title: Mehul Choksi's lawyer Vijay Aggarwal granted bail in UK pending trial on rape charge
articles.summary: A UK court on Wednesday granted bail to criminal lawyer Vijay Aggarwal, who has represented fugitive businessman Mehul Choksi, pending trial in a case
articles.body: A UK court on Wednesday granted bail to criminal lawyer Vijay Aggarwal, who has represented fugitive businessman Mehul Choksi, pending trial in a case involving allegations of rape and sexual assaults.Aggarwal, who represented Choksi in fraud and money laundering proceedings, had been lodged in a London prison after being charged. His bail was granted subject to what was described as one of the most “stringent packages of conditions ever offered”, including a substantial security bond and electronic tagging.Also Read: Mehul Choksi’s lawyer Vijay Aggarwal arrested in London and in prison accused of sexual assaultJustice David Tomlinson, presiding over the hearing at Southwark Crown Court, granted bail to Aggarwal and his co-accused, assistant Manpreet Kaur, following an application citing a “change in circumstances.”“I am minded to grant bail, given a significantly larger security for the male defendant,” Judge Tomlinson said.The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which had opposed bail in previous hearings, maintained its objection, describing Aggarwal as a “powerful person” with considerable influence and that both accused posed a flight risk. However, their lawyers successfully argued that the charges against them did not warrant continued detention.Aggarwal, 57, was granted bail to a UK address against a security bond of approximately £500,000. He will also be required to wear an electronic monitoring tag.Kaur, 41, offered a security bond of around £20,000 and will also be subject to strict monitoring conditions. Both have surrendered their passports to the UK police and are prohibited from travelling abroad until the trial, which is expected to take place next year.Aggarwal had previously been denied bail following his arrest in London in August. During subsequent court hearings, details emerged of allegations that he had engaged in non-consensual “sexual touching” of a woman and facilitated the travel of women with a “view to exploitation”.The lawyer, who was being held at Wandsworth Prison in south-west London, faces one charge of rape and three counts of sexual assault. His counsel argued that the rape allegation was not “straightforward” on the question of consent, pointing to police records in which the woman reportedly stated that she was “not a victim”. All women identified as key witnesses in the case have been granted anonymity under UK law.Aggarwal and Kaur were arrested on August 11 at a property on Brick Street in London's upscale Mayfair area over alleged sexual offences said to have taken place on May 26 and August 9.The property, located at 29 Brick Street, is listed online as the “Mayfair Residence Townhouse” and comprises multi-storey luxury apartments available for rent.(With PTI inputs)You use AI every day. articles.title: Downing Street's dancing TikToker Luke Hamnett defends visit
articles.summary: Luke Hamnett defends video of him mimicking the famous dance from film Love Actually.
articles.body:
An influencer has insisted his interview with the prime minister focused on serious issues, despite a backlash over his recreation of the famous dance from the film Love Actually.

Luke Hamnett, who has about 1.3 million followers on TikTok, spoke to Andy Burnham at Number 10 for an episode of his Live, Laugh, Luke podcast.

However, after posting the clip online, he - along with content creators including Max Balegde who attended a social media reception - were criticised in the media for turning Downing Street into a "laughing stock".

A spokesperson for the prime minister insisted that Burnham "absolutely respects" the history of 10 Downing Street.

Hamnett, from Stoke-on-Trent, told his followers that he had previously met Burnham in Manchester, and clarified that he was not in attendance at the creators' party, instead going to Downing Street alone with his parents and team for the podcast interview.

He wrote: "Whilst I did mention Larry The Cat (icon), the majority of the podcast episode involved questions and topics close to my heart personally - the cost of living crisis and growing up on a council estate, cancer treatment and diagnosis following my mum's recent recovery, the LGBTQ+ community and about my ADHD.

"Sadly none of these important topics or the PM's answers, made it to the news cycle which could have been the talking point."

"To be very clear, this wasn't a paid appearance or a paid visit. As a working-class man from Stoke, to get the chance to sit down with the prime minister one-on-one was a true privilege."

The video in which the former insurance salesman recreated Hugh Grant's prime ministerial dance from the film , was viewed more than 913,000 times on TikTok and amassed more than 121,000 likes.

The famous scene features Grant's character, the prime minister David, dancing through the rooms and hallways of Number 10 along to Girls Aloud's song Jump.

"The 'Love Actually' dance was simply a minute of fun, to promote the podcast - it was clearly light-hearted for the festive season and I believe, politics and those behind it can have lighter moments along with the very important and harder topics that exist for so many, including me," Hamnett added.

He continued: "There is a space and place for other political topics and global affairs to be discussed, I used my short time with the PM to discuss questions in relation to my lived experience.

"So many of you saw the great opportunity and positivity in both the podcast conversation and my Love Actually dance moves, so thank you for that love and support!"

Defending the decision to allow the clip to be filmed, Burnham's spokesperson said: "The Prime Minister has immense respect for No 10 Downing Street, but he also understands that there are millions of people now who don't get their news information from traditional media and they get their information from a variety of different channels.

"And he's determined to reach people where they are."

articles.title: Huang is back to corner office via couch: Tech boss talks therapy after return as CEO
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: For a man accustomed to making artificial intelligence smarter, Jensen Huang has concluded that a little work on his
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: For a man accustomed to making artificial intelligence smarter, Jensen Huang has concluded that a little work on his own emotional intelligence might not be a bad idea. Clawing his way back to the corner suite at Nvidia with help from MAGA boss Donald Trump following a spectacular fall from grace on account of his extra-marital capers, the contrite CEO told associates on Tuesday that he is undergoing daily therapy to confront his personal failings and become a better human being.At his first company-wide meeting after reinstatement on Tuesday, Huang reportedly acknowledged violating Nvidia's code of conduct and making serious personal mistakes -- including more affairs than had been previously reported -- that had hurt his wife and children. He described the meeting as the second-hardest of his life, after the conversation with his wife. He also conceded that his ferocious management style sometimes disempowered employees, while insisting that his intensity was central to Nvidia's success.The expressions of remorse came even as a deeply suspicious section of the American political establishment and a skeptical commentariat continued to ask probing questions about his rehabilitation. The unease -- even among Republican lawmakers -- grew after President Trump openly bragged about his intervention, arguing, “We have to protect our geniuses…we don’t have enough of them.” In the same interview (on CNBC), Trump also claimed he had “protected” Elon Musk during his first term after a “certain incident... a tough incident,” leading some analysts to allege he was acting more like a mob boss than the U.S President.In more cogent moments, Trump has suggested that personal foibles of some gifted individuals may have to be overlooked if the U.S is to maintain its tech lead over China, while describing Huang as a great patriot and national treasure. Critics have lit into what they see as a sketchy argument even as reports continue to surface about Huang’s toxic management style that prompted one commentator to note that he ran the world's most valuable company “like an Italian family restaurant.” The comparison was intended less as a compliment to the hospitality industry than as a critique on the absence of conventional corporate structures, succession planning, and clear separation between family and business in a critical cutting edge company where, his reaching for therapy notwithstanding, his daughter Madison and son-in-law Nico Caprez have influential roles.However, there is also a growing suspicion among some analysts that the timing and coordination of the “hits” on Jensen Huang -- including reports of his extra-marital affairs and abrasive style which apparently was common knowledge -- deserve greater scrutiny. In a series of posts, Anupam Chander, a professor of law and technology at Georgetown University, pointed out that reports on Huang’s managerial style did not bother to mention that he was #1 CEO in 2025 and 2026 in Glassdoor rankings, which are based on employee feedback. Others have pointed out that Huang’s peccadilloes had been reported more than a year ago but got no traction till someone decided to make it a hot button issue.Meanwhile, the political implications of the L’affaire Huang are starting to churn Washington, which is still digesting the stunning results from the mid-term polls. Marco Rubio, the China hawk whose intelligence concerns helped precipitate Huang's original departure, has found himself on the losing side of the White House argument, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who had publicly advocated finding an outside chief executive and demanded a shake-up at Nvidia, nimbly did a backflip after Trump rehabilitated Huang, saying, “Well, Jensen is on the outside now.” Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department had been criticised for its handling of the Megaspeed affair resulting in diverting Nvidia chips to China, has meanwhile survived the political storm. For now, the administration's China hawks have discovered that presidential displeasure can be a more immediate career threat than Chinese technological advances.Still, some Republican senators are showing signs of disquiet, although challenging Trump remains a hazardous occupation after spending years fawning over the boss. Outgoing Senate Intelligence Committee chairman Tom Cotton of Arkansas was particularly blunt, saying, “The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg,” while warning that Huang's reinstatement did not resolve the underlying national-security questions. At least half dozen GOP Senators have expressed unease over Nvidia-Huang ties to China.The larger question is whether any of these legislators will follow their words with action. The Trump White House has already demonstrated that even senior cabinet officials can be overruled when their positions collide with MAGA supremo's preferences.There is however one force more powerful than the President: the American voter, who has delivered Trump a brutal dressing-down in the midterm elections, handing Democrats control of the incoming Senate. The present Senate, which remains Republican-controlled until January, requires 67 votes to convict a president following impeachment. From January 2027, the Democratic-aligned bloc will number 56, leaving just 11 Republicans needed to reach the two-thirds threshold, assuming all 100 senators vote. While there is no imminent threat to Trump's presidency, it is a reminder that even presidential power has constitutional limits. Trump may be able to persuade a corporate board to restore its chief executive, but he can't be sure of his own political survival.For Huang, the immediate rehabilitation is complete, but the larger investigation is not. Nvidia says its independent inquiry into the foreign intelligence allegations will continue, and the company has established a new national-security and export-control committee. Congressional scrutiny of the company's China business is also gathering momentum. The man who returned to Nvidia with a promise to become a better CEO may therefore discover that therapy is the easiest part of his rehabilitation. The harder sessions will be before Congress, where neither a black leather jacket nor a presidential character reference is likely to substitute for answers about just where America's most powerful AI chips have ended up.You use AI every day. articles.title: Why are school shootings continuing to shake the Balkans?
articles.summary: A shooting in Serbia has renewed concerns over firearm access, online warning signs and failures to prevent violence.
articles.body:
A school shooting in central Serbia has renewed concerns about the availability of firearms, social media warning signs, and systemic failures, following a wave of similar violence across the Balkans.

On Tuesday, a 17-year-old suspect shot and wounded two school staff members at the First Technical School in Kragujevac, a city about 145km (90 miles) south of Belgrade.

Local media reported that the suspect, a student at the school, posted a photo posing with a rifle on social media hours before the attack.

The shooting began at about 8am (07:00 GMT) during the first class of the day.

According to the Kragujevac Police Department, a 17-year-old fourth-year student, identified by his initials V.M., brought a small-caliber rifle into the building and fired a shot towards the security reception desk.

A 50-year-old maintenance worker was struck in the leg, while another employee sustained leg injuries from shattered glass. Both victims were women and sustained lower limb injuries. After being treated in intensive care, they are now in a stable condition and out of danger.

A police patrol stationed nearby responded immediately, disarming and arresting the teenager while students and teachers were safely evacuated.

A juvenile judge at the Higher Court in Kragujevac ordered a 30-day detention for the suspect. The Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office has charged him with attempted aggravated murder and illegal possession and carrying of firearms. His father was also arrested on suspicion of keeping the rifle at home without a permit.

The school’s head teacher Nemanja Joksimovic and graduating students described the suspect as quiet, with no history of disciplinary issues.

Following the event, the school shortened class schedules and deployed counsellors and psychologists.

The photo of the suspect holding a rifle posted hours prior to the shooting has raised questions about online vigilance.

Nedzad Korajlic, a professor of criminology and safety studies at CEPS Kiseljak, said if other students see posts like this, they should immediately inform a parent, teacher, or trusted adult. In cases of a specific threat or immediate danger, the post should be saved and reported to the police and school leadership immediately, rather than forwarded across group chats, he said.

Korajlic added that adolescents often dismiss such posts as posturing or simply do not know who to contact. For that reason, schools must establish clear, confidential reporting protocols so students know exactly where to turn and what will happen next, he said.

What measures can be taken to prevent further attacks?

In response to previous attacks, governments across the Western Balkans have introduced school police officers, tightened entry controls, and installed security cameras.

However, Korajlic said prevention is key.

Schools should assign a designated safety officer and staff to evaluate reports. Law enforcement should be notified immediately if firearms or explicit threats are involved, with social and health services joining efforts as needed, he said.

The Kragujevac attack highlights the broader issue of widespread civilian firearm ownership in the region due to the availability of legal weapons and unregistered arms remaining from the 1990s Yugoslav wars.

Korajlic stressed that weapon storage regulations must be strictly enforced, meaning firearms must be locked away, ammunition kept separately, and keys or codes strictly inaccessible to minors.

Psychologist Goran Tomin told Serbia’s Beta news agency that shootings traumatise school communities, noting that institutional responses and sentencing policies are often too lenient. There is a high tolerance for violence in public discourse and the media, he said, while school counsellors are frequently overburdened with administrative work.

Following the attack, public officials pointed to digital content.

Zarko Micin, a mayor and politician, promised heightened security in local schools while singling out video games, as he urged parents to monitor media consumption.

But Korajlic cautioned against reducing complex incidents to cases of media consumption, noting that simply playing a violent video game tells us very little about a person’s real-world behaviour without analysing specific motives, context, and explicit threats.

Where else have shootings taken place in the Balkans?

Several shootings have shaken schools in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Croatia over the past three years.

The worst incident occurred in May 2023 at the Vladislav Ribnikar Elementary School in Belgrade . A 13-year-old student used his father’s handgun to kill nine classmates and a security guard, while wounding a teacher and five other students. Because he was under the legal age of criminal responsibility, he was placed in a psychiatric facility, while his father was sentenced to 14-and-a-half years in prison and his mother to three years.

Weeks later, a former student entered Lukavac Grad Elementary School in Bosnia with a firearm, critically wounding an English teacher. The suspect was sentenced to detention in a juvenile correctional facility, while his father was prosecuted for illegal weapon possession and child neglect.

In August 2024, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a school custodian armed with an automatic rifle killed three staff , including the head teacher. He then attempted suicide at the Sanski Most Mixed Secondary School but survived. The 61-year-old suspect was indicted for triple murder and illegal weapons possession.

The wave of violence also extended to Croatia. In December 2024, a 19-year-old former pupil entered Precko Elementary School in Zagreb with a knife, killing a seven-year-old pupil and severely injuring a teacher and three children. The suspect was charged with aggravated murder and attempted murder, prompting Croatian authorities to mandate locked school doors and professional security personnel.

Korajlic told Al Jazeera that true safety will remain out of reach until early prevention, youth mental health support, and strict home firearm controls are prioritised across society.

articles.summary: The closure came after North Korea condemned Switzerland for adding a children’s camp to its sanctions list.
articles.body:
The Swiss government has said it regretted North Korea’s decision to close Switzerland’s diplomatic office in Pyongyang in a spat over sanctions just weeks after Bern reopened its office in the North Korean capital.

Switzerland’s Federal Department of Foreign Affairs said it was officially informed earlier on Wednesday of the North Korean authorities’ decision to close the Swiss diplomatic office.

On Tuesday, North Korea condemned Switzerland for adding a children’s camp to its sanctions list over Western allegations that it was involved in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine and said it would consider shutting down the diplomatic office in Pyongyang.

“The [foreign ministry] regrets this decision and is arranging for the Head of the Office to return to the Embassy of Switzerland in Beijing,” the Swiss ministry said in a statement.

North Korea ordered the envoy to leave within 48 hours, its Foreign Ministry said.

In a statement carried by the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), the ministry said the move was in response to Switzerland’s decision to impose sanctions on North Korea’s Songdowon International Children’s Camp, calling it an overtly hostile act.

Pyongyang’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs summoned the head of the diplomatic office, Sylvain Astier, and handed him a memorandum urging him to close the office, KCNA said.

“The Foreign Ministry of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea [DPRK] declared the head of the Swiss Diplomatic Office in the DPRK persona non grata and urged him to leave the country within 48 hours,” KCNA said, using the country’s official name.

“Any act of violating the sovereign rights of the DPRK and the interests of its citizens can never be welcomed by us,” it said.

The expulsion comes less than a month after Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis formally reopened the diplomatic office in Pyongyang.

The sanctions infringed on North Korea’s sovereignty by denying what was its obligation to provide children with opportunities for culture and recreation, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un’s influential sister, Kim Yo Jong, said.

Switzerland’s Federal Department of Foreign Affairs defended its sanctions policy on Tuesday, saying it was independent of the reopening of the diplomatic office, which it said was carried out “in line with our universalist foreign policy”.

“Its aim is to maintain channels of dialogue, including with states with which we have differences on certain issues,” it told the Reuters news agency.

Over the weekend, Kim Jong Un personally received credentials from the new ambassadors of 10 countries, including Russia and Sweden, in a rare diplomatic ceremony in Pyongyang.

Kim said North Korea sought to expand foreign relations with countries that respected its sovereignty, but would oppose attempts to restrict the independent rights and right to development of sovereign states.

Switzerland established diplomatic relations with North Korea in 1974 and is one of the few Western countries to maintain dialogue with the country. Both Kim Jong Un and Kim Yo Jong reportedly attended school in Switzerland as teenagers in the 1990s.

Meanwhile, North Korea has closely aligned with Russia over the war in Ukraine, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons in recent years to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion, possibly in exchange for aid and military technology transfers.

articles.title: Gordon Ramsay to host Top Gear as show revived after Andrew Flintoff crash
articles.summary: Ramsay will take the driving seat alongside as yet unnamed co-presenters when the show starts filming next year.
articles.body:
TV chef Gordon Ramsay is to lead the new presenting line-up on BBC motoring show Top Gear, which is being revived four years after it was last on air.

Ramsay will take the driving seat alongside as yet unnamed co-presenters when the show starts filming next year. It will return to screens in 2028.

The long-running programme has been off air since 2022, when co-host Andrew Flintoff suffered serious facial and rib injuries after his open-topped three-wheeled car overturned at the show's test-track.

In a statement announcing his new role, Ramsay said he wants to bring "a fresh energy and ambition" to the show's formula of being "surprising, entertaining and [with] just the right amount of chaos".

Top Gear began in 1977 and became one of the BBC's biggest hits in the hands of Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May in the 2000s.

They were replaced by hosts including Chris Evans and Friends star Matt LeBlanc, before Flintoff took over in 2018 with Paddy McGuinness and Chris Harris.

But the show was "rested" after the former cricketer's crash in December 2022.

Flintoff was dragged face-down underneath the Morgan Super 3 car for about 50 metres. "I thought I was dead," he told a Disney+ documentary last year.

The BBC apologised and paid compensation to Flintoff following his crash.

In Wednesday's statement, Ramsay said he has had a love of cars since he grew up near the Silverstone race circuit in Northamptonshire.

"I would climb over the fences and sneak in for a glimpse of the racing," he said. "That early excitement sparked a lifelong passion for cars, motor sport, beautiful design and extraordinary engineering.

"At its very best Top Gear has always been about the unexpected - surprising, entertaining and just the right amount of chaos.

"That's the spirit we want to build on, bringing a fresh energy and ambition to create something truly thrilling for a whole new generation of audiences.

"It's an incredibly exciting opportunity, and I genuinely can't wait to get started!"

Former host Richard Hammond told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that Top Gear is "a grand old BBC stalwart".

"It goes back decades. We had our tenure of it and did our thing with it and went a bit crazy with it, and it'll be another incarnation of it," he said. "And great. It's a long runner, it'll carry on."

He said that he does not doubt Ramsay's credentials as a car fan, and joked that TV chefs "love three things: cooking - well in his case four - swearing, cooking, but also big watches and cars".

Hammond was seriously injured in a crash while filming the show in 2006, but said it "doesn't have to be" a dangerous show.

The BBC asked Hammond to return to the show for the new series, he said.

"They did talk to me about it. They came to me about maybe getting involved in leading the new Top Gear, and I don't want to drag it back to what it was. That's why I didn't do it," he said.

Ramsay, 60, owns an extensive collection of cars including multiple Aston Martins and Ferraris, as well as a Porsche, Land Rover and McLaren Senna.

He has also appeared on Top Gear three times as a guest - in 2002, 2006 and 2017.

The BBC's director of entertainment Ed Havard said: "Gordon's fierce and fearless approach makes him a natural fit, and we're thrilled that audiences will see him in the driving seat as the show speeds into its next exciting era."

Suzy Lamb, managing director for BBC Studios Entertainment, added: "The return of Top Gear had to feel like a real TV event and Gordon fits the bill perfectly.

"He brings passion, mischief, genuine motoring credibility, and the kind of infectious competitive streak that defines the show at its best."

She promised that it "won't be a nostalgic reboot" but will be a "bold and unmissable new chapter for the most entertaining motoring show in the world".

Comedian Jimmy Carr was rumoured to have been in talks to join the hosting line-up, but was reported on Tuesday to have "pulled out".

Top Gear is the second high-profile show involving Ramsay to have been announced in the past week.

He has also been confirmed to star in a revival of Hell's Kitchen on ITV, hosted by Claudia Winkleman, more than two decades after he originally appeared on the celebrity cooking programme.

articles.title: Mississippi plane crash victims were members of a Florida family returning from a fishing trip
articles.summary: A deadly plane crash off the coast of Mississippi claimed the lives of six members of a southwest Florida family who were flying home from Louisiana after a fishing trip, officials confirmed Wednesday.
articles.body: A deadly plane crash off the coast of Mississippi claimed the lives of six members of a southwest Florida family who were flying home from Louisiana after a fishing trip, officials confirmed Wednesday. They were identified as Brent Stokes, 50, Michael Knox, 43, Arlyn Knox, 43, Charles Holden Knox, 12, Truett Knox, 10, and Hunter Stokes, 16. The names were confirmed by the plane’s owner, Rhonda Culmer. They all lived in Fort Myers, Florida, records show. “They died doing what they loved: celebrating the start of a wonderful holiday season with a fishing trip together, before heading home to be with the rest of our family,” the family said in a statement obtained by NBC affiliate WBBH-TV. “In the middle of our grief, we are holding on to that, and to how much love they gave us and how much love surrounds us now. We will carry them with us always.” The plane was piloted by Brent Stokes, according to WBBH-TV. Stokes, according to available records, is president of a Fort Myers marine construction company called Stokes Marine. He was the father of Hunter Stokes, according to Bruce Lynd Jr., the Jackson County, Mississippi, coroner. Stokes was also the brother of Arlyn Knox, who ran a local IT company with her husband, Michael Knox, called Knox Technology. Charles and Truett were their sons, the coroner said. Knox Technology declined to comment. The family had been in Louisiana on a fishing trip and was flying home to Fort Myers. Their single-engine Cesna took off from New Orleans Lakefront Airport about 2 p.m. local time on Tuesday, officials said. The plane went down around 3:30 p.m. some two 2 miles northeast of Horn Island, the Coast Guard said. “That’s when they lost communication,” said Juan Ros, a Coast Guard public affairs officer, adding that radar showed the plane descending “at 10,000 feet per minute.” Divers from the Mississippi Department of Marine Resources found the victims in the plane’s fuselage, the Coast Guard’s Heartland District office in New Orleans said in a statement Tuesday night. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the crash. “We are deeply grateful to the U.S. Coast Guard, the Mississippi Department of Marine Resources, and everyone who searched for and brought our family home,” the family said in its statement. “We also thank everyone who has reached out with prayers and kindness.” Photos from Arlyn Knox’s Facebook account show that the family appeared to share a love of sports and traveling. The pictures show the Knox children, Charles Holden Knox and Truett Knox, playing in local soccer, baseball and basketball little leagues. The family also seemed to root for the University of Florida Gators, according to images. The family took trips to the Bahamas, the mountains of North Carolina and Savannah, Georgia last summer, according to the account. In January, Arlyn Knox shared photos of her and her husband, Michael Knox, in honor of their 12th wedding anniversary. The photos show the young couple posing by a body of water and kissing under fireworks. In December 2023, Arlyn Knox posted several photos appearing to show her Michael Knox in the cockpit of a small plane with her two children. “One year ago he said he wanted to become a pilot, and today he passed his check ride!!” she wrote. “We love you!”

articles.title: Nigeria’s Tinubu pledges to bring peace to rebellion-hit border region
articles.summary: Tinubu is under pressure to convince voters that military operations in the country’s northeast will deliver security.
articles.body:
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu promised supporters in the northeastern city ⁠of Maiduguri he would restore peace to their rebellion-hit region, as an election looms in January.

Tinubu made the pledge at a rally in the city on Wednesday, as he seeks a second and final term in an election on January 16.

Maiduguri is the capital of Borno State , the heartland ⁠of the rebellion led by Boko Haram and ISIL West Africa Province (ISWAP).

Tinubu is under pressure to convince voters that intensified military operations in Borno and the northwest, where kidnapping for ransom remains rife, will deliver lasting security gains for communities scarred ‌by conflict.

“We will achieve that peace; the terrorism will go; they [rebel fighters] have the opportunity now to lay down their arms, to lay down all arms and surrender all weapons, change from the character of terrorism and banditry,” Tinubu said.

Holding the rally in Maiduguri sent a “simple statement saying there’s an improvement in the security situation”, Kabir Adamu, the managing director at Beacon Security and Innovations Limited, told Al Jazeera.

It also showed “an improvement … in the economic circumstances within the state”, Adamu said, speaking from Nigeria’s capital of Abuja.

Tinubu’s main rivals are former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, a former Anambra State governor who won more than 6 million votes in the last election.

Insecurity remains despite some progress

Ending insecurity in the north was one of Tinubu’s promises when campaigning for the presidency ⁠in 2023, but analysts and his opponents say that, like his predecessors, ⁠he has fallen short.

More than 50 percent of respondents disapprove of the president’s performance and more than 70 percent rate the economy “poor or very poor”, according to a YIAGA Africa poll released in October.

But Adamu said, “significant progress” has been made within Borno State.

“There was a time when about 24 local governments were more or less being contested, in terms of their control by the state or non-state actors,” he explained.

“Now, reasonably, almost all the local governments are accessible, even though there are challenges outside the immediate city centres.”

Nigeria’s defence minister said this month that the military was receiving real-time ⁠US intelligence and satellite support to target armed group leaders and degrade rebel networks.

In May, US and Nigerian forces led a mission that killed Abu-Bilal al-Minuki, ⁠ISIL’s global second-in-command.

Security analysts say Nigerian forces have driven ⁠rebels from most of the territory they once held, but the fighters still stage deadly raids, ambushes and bombings.

The armed groups have also been increasing their activities in the northwest, where kidnapping gangs mostly operate.

Crisis monitoring group ACLED said earlier this year that fighters ‌linked to al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS) were rapidly increasing their attacks on the borderlands between Niger, Benin and Nigeria, turning remote transit corridors into active conflict zones.

Tinubu said security forces were working to ‌rescue ‌more than 70 schoolchildren who remain in captivity after being abducted in two separate attacks in May and June in Borno.

Another key issue in the run-up to the elections is economic reform, as poverty has increased and access to basic commodities is increasingly difficult, said Adamu.

articles.title: Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court cancels power company contract as many wonder what’s next
articles.summary: The ruling made public Wednesday plunges the island into further uncertainty as many wonder who will take over from Luma  Energy while power outages persist.
articles.body: SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico — Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court has narrowly ruled in favor of canceling the government’s contract with Luma Energy following a contentious legal fight with the private power company. The 5-4 ruling made public Wednesday plunges the island into further uncertainty as many wonder who will take over from Luma while power outages persist across the U.S. territory and crews continue to repair the grid razed by Hurricane Maria in 2017. Puerto Rico’s government had awarded a multimillion-dollar contract to Luma, which took over the transmission and distribution of power on the island in June 2021. It inherited infrastructure that was crumbling after decades of neglect and mismanagement under Puerto Rico’s Electric Power Authority. The company said in a statement Wednesday that it disagrees with the court’s decision but will respect the judicial process and is “carefully evaluating all available legal alternatives.” “We remain concerned about the potential impact of this decision on ongoing efforts to strengthen and modernize Puerto Rico’s electric grid,” Luma said. “This matter goes beyond a contractual dispute. It has significant implications for the provision of an essential electric service, public safety, and Puerto Rico’s energy future.” Luma is a consortium made up of Calgary, Alberta-based Atco and Quanta Services Inc. of Houston. Puerto Rico’s government sued Luma nearly a year ago, following up on a campaign promise made by Gov. Jenniffer González to cancel the contract. In December 2025, González said Luma had nearly $11 billion in federal funds at its disposal to rebuild the grid, but that it has only been able to recover some $550 million in reimbursements from the U.S. Federal Emergency Management Agency. When the lawsuit was filed, she said, “Despite the operator’s expectations and representations, the electrical system has not improved with the speed, consistency or effectiveness that Puerto Rico deserves and that LUMA promised and lied to us about.” Puerto Rico’s government has two main agreements with Luma: one for operation and maintenance, and a supplemental deal that was needed because the state-owned Electric Power Authority has not yet started a debt restructuring process. The island’s power company remains mired in that process. Both deals were set to expire in November 2022, prompting the government to extend the supplemental agreement via an extension letter. González has said that the letter granted LUMA indefinite control, and that the extension granted was “in violation of the law and the principles of sound public administration.” The ongoing outages have also been blamed on Genera PR, a private company that oversees the generation of power on the island.

articles.title: In 1925, a Canadian family began farming in southern Alberta; 101 years later, descendants have donated 160 acres of native grassland that will remain protected while ranchers continue grazing cattle
articles.summary: A ranching family in southern Alberta has donated 160 acres of untouched native prairie for permanent protection, more than 100 years after first settling
articles.body: A ranching family in southern Alberta has donated 160 acres of untouched native prairie for permanent protection, more than 100 years after first settling in the region. The land will remain open for cattle grazing, allowing the family’s farming tradition to continue while protecting the natural grassland. The Nature Conservancy of Canada (NCC) announced on 24 November 2026 that the Coppieters family had donated the 65-hectare property, known as Coppieters Acres, along Alberta's Milk River Ridge. The land is located 17 kilometres southeast of Magrath in Warner County. It will remain protected as native fescue grassland while continuing to support local ranching."Peter and I have always really appreciated and looked up to people who chose to conserve their land. When we talked about it, we thought this was the best thing we could do with the quarter pasture. We're happy that it will stay the way it's always been," land donor Donna Coppieters said in the Nature Conservancy of Canada announcement.A century of family stewardshipThe family has long referred to the property as the "quarter pasture". Peter Coppieters Sr. and his wife, Mary, first settled in the region in 1925. They bought land and started the family farm. Their son, Peter, later bought the quarter pasture with his wife, Donna, continuing the family's care for the property. The land has never been ploughed or used for crops. It has remained natural prairie, where cattle graze and generations of the family have made memories. Donna Coppieters said the property is home to a wide range of wildlife, including elk, deer, pronghorn and many types of birds. Protecting the land will preserve both an important part of the family's history and an area of native prairie for future generations.Milk River Ridge and threatened grasslandsCoppieters Acres lies along the Milk River Ridge, which follows Alberta's southern border between Magrath and Milk River. The area is an important refuge for foothills rough fescue grassland, one of Alberta's most threatened natural ecosystems. Around 80 per cent of the remaining foothills rough fescue ecosystem is on privately owned land. This makes voluntary conservation efforts by landowners especially important. According to the Nature Conservancy of Canada, the donation builds on earlier conservation work in the region supported by its donors, including McIntyre Ranch and Sandstone Ranch. Water collected along the Milk River Ridge supplies communities and farms across central North America. Water flowing north enters the Oldman watershed and moves across the Prairies towards Hudson Bay. Water flowing south enters the Milk River watershed before travelling through the Missouri and Mississippi rivers to the Gulf of Mexico.Wildlife and carbon storage on the landAbout 87 per cent of the 65-hectare property is covered by native fescue grassland. The remaining area consists of wetlands and areas beside rivers and streams. These natural areas help store and filter water before it reaches downstream watersheds. Field surveys conducted in 2026 recorded bobolinks on the property. The bird is listed as a species of special concern in Canada, and its Canadian population has fallen by about 80 per cent since 1970, according to the Nature Conservancy of Canada. Survey teams also confirmed the presence of hoary bats and silver-haired bats. Both are listed as sensitive in Alberta and have been recommended for Endangered status by the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada (COSEWIC). Five other species of concern, all listed as sensitive in Alberta, were also recorded in the project area. They are Brewer's sparrow, eastern kingbird, plains garter snake, sharp-tailed grouse and upland sandpiper.The protected prairie also provides benefits beyond wildlife habitat. Natural grasslands help filter water and support pollinating insects. These insects contribute an estimated $3 billion each year in ecosystem service value to prairie crop production, according to the Nature Conservancy of Canada. Alberta's native fescue grasslands also store large amounts of carbon. They can hold up to 200 tonnes of carbon per hectare in the top metre of soil. The Nature Conservancy of Canada estimates that about 11,400 tonnes of carbon are stored beneath Coppieters Acres. This is similar to the annual emissions produced by nearly 14,000 cars. The wider loss of prairie grasslands has also been significant. Figures from the Nature Conservancy of Canada show that Canada has lost more than 80 per cent of its prairie grasslands since European settlement. Around 60,000 hectares are still lost each year, while less than 6 per cent of the remaining grasslands are formally protected.Grazing stays part of the planThe donation combines permanent protection of the natural habitat with continued ranching. Carefully managed cattle grazing helps keep prairie landscapes open, supports a variety of native plants and contributes to the rural economy."Milk River Ridge is one of the most intact grassland landscapes left in Alberta, and every hectare that stays whole matters. The Coppieters family's gift is exactly the kind of local stewardship that keeps these grasslands healthy, working and connected for the ranchers, wildlife and communities who depend on them," said Tom Lynch-Staunton, regional vice president for the Nature Conservancy of Canada.The organisation's stewardship staff will assess the property and prepare a management plan to guide future grazing. This will include checking the health of the grassland and managing invasive species. The Nature Conservancy of Canada said the project was made possible by the Coppieters family, with support from Cenovus through the Conserving Critical Wetlands Program.You use AI every day. articles.title: Terrorists’ properties attached in J&K’s Reasi, Handwara
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: J&K Police attached 29 kanals (1 kanal = 5445sqft) of land belonging to five Pakistan-based terrorist handlers in Reasi district, officials said
articles.body: SRINAGAR: J&K Police attached 29 kanals (1 kanal = 5445sqft) of land belonging to five Pakistan-based terrorist handlers in Reasi district, officials said Wednesday.In a separate action in Kupwara district, police attached land measuring five kanals and 12 marlas at Chogul, Handwara, belonging to two proclaimed offenders — Fayaz Ahmad Khan and Shameem Ahmad — based in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, police said.The action in Reasi stemmed from an FIR registered at Mahore PS under relevant sections of the BNS, Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, and the E&IMCO Act. Police said the owners of these properties — Mohammad Qayoom, Bashir Ahmed, Shokat Ali, Manzoor Ahmed, and Imtyaz Ahmed — had exfiltrated to Pakistan for terrorist training and were currently operating as terrorist handlers from across the border. Investigation revealed the five were allegedly involved in directing, facilitating and coordinating terrorist activities in J&K in a bid to revive terrorism in the Union Territory. They were also trying to sell these properties and channel the proceeds into financing and sustaining subversive activities in the region, police said.Reasi Police identified and verified the assets in coordination with the revenue department. After investigation and completion of the requisite formalities, J&K DGP approved the attachment proceedings, police said.Meanwhile, J&K Police, in coordination with other security agencies, conducted anti-terror drills in south Kashmir’s Kulgam district, where forces had gunned down Lashkar-e-Taiba commander Mohammad Lateef Bhat in an encounter on Nov 18. Police said Bhat was the last known active local terrorist in Kashmir.Police said the drills — carried out under the critical incident response system in Kulgam town, Chawalgam, and Larnoo — were meant to assess operational preparedness, response capabilities, and coordination among various security agencies in handling critical situations and emergencies.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Surrey County Council adopts first formal policy on AI use
articles.summary: Surrey County Council's policy sets out rules and safeguarding around the council's use of AI tools.
articles.body:
A council has adopted its first formal policy on artificial intelligence (AI), with the aim of regulating use of the technology.

The policy sets out rules and safeguarding around the council's use of AI, including that any AI tool used must be authorised for use by the authority.

Councillors and officers will not be allowed to use AI software accessed via the internet, such as Gemini or ChatGPT, over data security concerns, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said.

The policy states anyone using AI for council business must do so in a way that is "safe, ethical, lawful and appropriate".

Councillor David Lewis said: "We do want to make sure that we operate AI in a safe and responsible manner, but at the same time, we have to make sure that we have the right safeguards in place."

He added: "We have to be careful that we don't put so many controls in place that we actually impede and hinder our use of AI going forward, providing that's done in a responsible way."

Approved tasks for AI assistance include administrative assistance and data analysis.

Prohibited areas include removing human oversight from decisions that affect residents, unfair discrimination and generating misleading information with the help of AI.

Any AI use that breaches data protection, confidentiality or security rules will also be banned.

The policy states any breaches of the rules would be treated as misconduct, which could lead to disciplinary action or dismissal for employees and "contractual consequences" for contractors or agency workers.

articles.title: Vande Mataram at J&K waqf event sparks row
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: Several Muslim clerics who attended a J&K Waqf Board function where Vande Mataram was played in full expressed regret and said they had prayed
articles.body: SRINAGAR: Several Muslim clerics who attended a J&K Waqf Board function where Vande Mataram was played in full expressed regret and said they had prayed for repentance, as the national song triggered a religious controversy in Kashmir.The clerics, who attended Monday’s Waqf Day event in Srinagar, said they had neither endorsed the song in their hearts nor through their words. “Since we attended the gathering, if our participation has hurt anyone’s religious sentiments, we sincerely repent before Allah and pray that He accepts our repentance,” they said in a statement on Wednesday.The function was attended by Union minority affairs minister Kiren Rijiju, waqf board chairperson and senior BJP politician Dr Darakhshan Andrabi, Lok Sabha MP Mian Altaf Ahmad and other dignitaries.All six stanzas of Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay’s 1875 poem Vande Mataram were played at the event in accordance with a Union home ministry protocol directive issued earlier this year that mandated the full version at state functions, official events and legislature sessions.In August, the President cleared the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Act, putting Vande Mataram on a par with the national anthem. The amendment did not alter the stanzas, but made disrespect or disruption punishable.Adopted as a slogan during the freedom movement, the poem was abridged in 1937 when the Congress Working Committee approved only its first two stanzas to respect religious diversity.Mirwaiz Umar Farooq-led Mutahida Majlis-e-Ulama (MMU), an amalgam of religious organisations and institutions, said there was no legal obligation to play the song at an official function, and criticised the waqf board for playing it at an event organised by an institution entrusted with safeguarding Muslim religious endowments.It said playing Vande Mataram at the event conflicted with Islam’s principle of Tawheed, or absolute oneness of Allah. “While Islam encourages love for one’s homeland, it draws a clear distinction between love for one’s homeland and its worship. Any expression or practice that attributes divinity to the motherland is contrary to the fundamental Islamic belief of Tawheed and is, therefore, un-Islamic and impermissible for Muslims,” MMU said.It said it was considering legal advice and urged Muslims entrusted with religious responsibilities to uphold their beliefs without compromise. Andrabi was not available for comment.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
