articles.title: UK military ‘moving aircraft to hangars in case of drone attacks’
articles.summary: Experts say the move is a ‘logical response’ if there is intelligence suggesting a likely drone threat.
articles.body:
Britain’s Ministry of Defence (MoD) says it takes “the security of our bases, equipment and personnel very seriously,” after media outlets reported the Royal Air Force (RAF) had taken new precautions against possible drone attacks.

The Times and Sky News reported on Wednesday that planes would be moved to hangars and hardened shelters overnight, and anti-drone nets would be installed to protect any warplanes that remained exposed.

The MoD did not confirm the reports, but in a statement said it was “always adapting to counter any potential threats”.

Justin Bronk, a senior researcher at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) think tank in London, told Al Jazeera that the RAF’s reported tactics would be “a sensible, logical response if there is intelligence suggesting a likely drone threat”.

“The main bases used for RAF fighters, Coningsby, Marham and Lossiemouth all still have hardened aircraft shelters from the Cold War era that have been maintained in usable condition for both aircraft storage, protection and limited maintenance work,” Bronk said.

However, Bronk cautioned that there were not enough hardened shelters to protect all of the jets at each airbase, after squadrons were consolidated into ‘super bases’ following the end of the Cold War, and a “mistaken assumption” that such protection was no longer important.

The MoD said it was investing an additional 470 million pounds ($615m) “to strengthen security at military sites, including better physical protection, surveillance and counter-drone capabilities”, and that 15 million pounds ($19.6m) had already been invested “in drone and counter-drone technology and introduced restricted airspace over 44 critical Defence sites”.

British authorities have regularly issued warnings about threats posed by Russia and Iran, and the government has urged the country to be prepared for different contingencies. In a report in October, members of Parliament warned that Britain’s military needed to make “dramatic progress” to be ready for a potential attack by Russia on a NATO country.

On Tuesday, Britain’s domestic MI5 intelligence service and the MoD issued a joint alert warning UK military suppliers to Ukraine about increasing sabotage attempts by Russia.

“Aircraft inside a standard hangar or a hardened aircraft shelter are protected from attacks by infiltrated adversary cells or terrorists with small drones,” explained RUSI’s Justin Bronk. “But only those in hardened shelters are protected from larger one-way attack drones like the Geran 2/3/4 series during a hypothetical wartime attack,” he added, referring to the Geran drones manufactured and operated by Russia, based on an original Iranian design.

Bronk said that even though hardened aircraft shelters seem old-fashioned, they are a “relatively low-risk, inexpensive and effective way to improve fighter fleet resilience in wartime.”

“They provide almost total protection from drones due to thick concrete and blast doors, and also mean that any unintercepted cruise missile can only destroy a single jet at most with a direct hit.”

Earlier this month US forces responded to possible unauthorised drone activity over a military base in the United Kingdom, hosting American warplanes.

“No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected” at the eastern RAF Lakenheath base, a US Air Force spokesperson said in a statement at the time.

There was also an Iran-linked security scare on September 27 at the southwestern RAF Fairford base, which was used by the US planes. A group of men allegedly drove three vans up to a village near the site and abandoned them with filled petrol barrels inside, sparking a bomb scare and evacuation.

Washington had used the airbase in its war on Iran, and days after the September incident withdrew all its B-1 bombers from the base. Two men have since been charged in a UK court over the incident, and three in the United States.

The US military also withdrew its planes from RAF Mildenhall, near Lakenheath, on November 9 , following a threat from Iran, according to The Wall Street Journal and The Financial Times.

articles.title: Could renewed strikes on Hodeidah port worsen Yemen’s humanitarian crisis?
articles.summary: Disruptions at Yemen’s largest seaport could exacerbate hardships for millions of Yemenis, aid experts warn.
articles.body:
The Saudi-led coalition has launched renewed attacks on Houthi targets at Yemen’s port of Hodeidah as the armed group fights Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

The strikes come amid significant Houthi territorial gains in recent weeks and escalating attacks by the group on Saudi Arabia.

Hodeidah, which has repeatedly been attacked over the past decade, is critical to both Yemen’s economy and the supply of essential goods to millions of people in Houthi-controlled areas.

The port of Hodeidah, situated on Yemen’s western Red Sea coast, is the country’s principal commercial seaport and has been under Houthi control since 2014.

It serves as a major entry point for food, fuel and other commercial goods as well as humanitarian assistance, supplying the densely populated northern and western regions of Yemen, including the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa.

The port had eight berths and the capacity to accommodate 6,500 standard shipping containers in 2023. However, attrition due to Yemen’s more than a decade of conflict has reduced the number of operational berths and damaged cranes and storage facilities.

Despite this, in September 2025, the United Nations Mission to Support the Hodeidah Agreement estimated that the port handled about 70 percent of commercial imports and 80 percent of humanitarian aid coming into Yemen, calling it a “lifeline”.

“The closure or disruption [of the port] under the current circumstances would delay the arrival of food, medicine and fuel; increase transport costs and prices; and exacerbate the suffering of families already facing an acute humanitarian crisis,” said Abdusattor Esoev, Yemen Chief of Mission for the International Organization for Migration.

“At a time when millions of people in Yemen depend on humanitarian assistance and face severe food insecurity, Hodeidah remains a critical lifeline. The port is essential for bringing in food, fuel, medicines and other basic goods needed by civilians across northern Yemen,” said Francesca Quinto, the programme manager for Yemen for Doctors Without Borders.

However, the Houthis have long been accused of using Hodeidah’s port for both civilian and military purposes. Investigations have found that the group exploits commercial port facilities to smuggle in weapons from Iran, its chief ally.

“The ports of Hodeidah are key to commercial flows. However, the Houthis’ increasing militarisation of vital civilian infrastructure by smuggling and storing arms, fuel and narcotics is undermining the humanitarian functions they serve in wartime,” Ibrahim Jalal, a senior researcher and policy adviser, told Al Jazeera.

Tawfiq al-Hamidi, a Yemeni lawyer and human rights activist, told Al Jazeera that the port has been misused by the group for smuggling despite its importance for Yemen’s population.

“Nevertheless, efforts must be made to protect the port as a civilian facility, and the Houthi movement must provide genuine guarantees,” he said.

Yes. Since the start of Yemen’s civil war in September 2014, the port and its surrounding area have repeatedly come under attack from the Saudi-led coalition, the United States, the United Kingdom and Israel. Pro-Yemeni government forces also tried to capture it in a 2018 offensive.

About 70 percent of Yemenis live in Houthi-controlled areas in the country’s west, where most goods arrive from the rest of the world through Red Sea ports. Humanitarian aid continues to enter through other ports, including Mocha and a major government-held port in Aden, but renewed fighting has made the overland flow of this aid to the country’s interior difficult. Humanitarian operations in Houthi-controlled areas have also been severely curtailed because of the detention of UN staff by the group.

In March 2015, shortly after launching its military intervention in support of the Yemeni government, the Saudi-led coalition began a partial maritime blockade on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen.

A UN-brokered nationwide truce in April 2022 led to an easing of restrictions on fuel imports through Hodeidah. Further restrictions on commercial imports were lifted in early 2023, which also helped to revitalise the port.

But that recovery was then jeopardised by a campaign of US, British and Israeli strikes on Houthi-controlled areas beginning in 2024 and lasting into the next year, in retaliation for Houthi drone and missile attacks on Israel and Red Sea shipping, carried out ostensibly in the name of supporting Gaza during Israel’s genocidal war on the Palestinian enclave.

Why is Saudi Arabia attacking the port now?

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen announced on Wednesday that it had launched new strikes against the Houthis at the port, days after it warned civilians to evacuate the area. The Houthis have promised not to let strikes against the port go unanswered.

Since the return of full-scale war to Yemen in September, the Houthis have made sweeping territorial gains across Yemen, pushing back the forces of the internationally recognised government.

A government counteroffensive launched in early October has failed to stem Houthi advances despite heavy air support. Government forces are now scrambling to defend Aden , the interim capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

“Broadly speaking, the strikes [on Hodeidah’s port] were a response to the shift on the battlefield in favour of the Houthis,” Ali al-Dhahab, a Yemeni military and strategic analyst, told Al Jazeera.”

“They were aimed at undermining and crippling their economic and logistical capabilities, including infrastructure, such as ports and airports, as well as their military capabilities,” he said.

Escalating Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia targeting airports, oil infrastructure and commercial buildings also played a role in the decision, al-Dhahab said, mentioning Thursday’s attack on the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund in Riyadh.

The following day, the Saudi-led coalition urged civilians near Hodeidah’s port to evacuate without providing specifics.

Before Wednesday’s strikes, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree reiterated a threat of retaliation on Saudi seaports on the Red Sea, naming Jeddah’s port in particular.

Nabil Al-Bukairi, a Yemeni researcher and policy expert, told Al Jazeera that Saudi Arabia’s strikes on the port should not be taken as a warning. “I believe the strikes have gone beyond being merely symbolic,” he said.

“Continued bombardment would inevitably lead to its closure and render it inoperable once its infrastructure and logistical capabilities have been targeted,” he warned.

Even without a closure, strikes that disrupt the operations of the facility risk delays of critical aid as Yemen’s war shows no sign of an imminent end.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy retrial moves forward as state's highest court denies prosecutors' request to pause murder case
articles.summary: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court denied prosecutors' bid to pause Lindsay Clancy's murder case as her double jeopardy appeal is considered.
articles.body: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court rejected prosecutors' request to delay Lindsay Clancy's murder retrial while it considers a double jeopardy appeal filed by her defense attorneys. Prosecutors with the Plymouth County District Attorney's Office filed a motion Monday seeking to pause proceedings in Clancy's murder case, arguing it would be "ambitious" to expect the state's highest court to resolve her double jeopardy appeal before jury selection begins March 29. Clancy is accused of strangling her three young children to death. "The full Court will presumably determine whether such a retrial will violate the defendant’s double jeopardy rights," Assistant Plymouth County District Attorney Melissa Johnsen wrote. "As such, it makes little sense to move forward with proceedings intended to bring the defendant to a trial, where this Court may ultimately decide that a retrial is barred by double jeopardy." LINDSAY CLANCY PROSECUTORS ASK COURT TO DELAY HER RETRIAL IN CHILDREN'S STRANGLINGS The motion was denied without explanation by Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court justices. Clancy's lawyers, Kevin Reddington and Martin Weinberg, opposed the motion, stating in a reply to the state's motion that "she wants to keep her trial date." LINDSAY CLANCY TO BE RETRIED FOR MURDER IN KILLING OF THREE CHILDREN READ THE MOTION: Clancy, 36, faces murder charges in the deaths of her children — Cora, Dawson and Callan — all under age 6, who were found strangled at the family's home in January 2023. Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial Sept. 4 after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict, ending in an 11-1 divide. SEND US A TIP Prosecutors argued a stay would "forego any additional expense and effort" in preparations, while Clancy's lawyers said, "The cost of a stay would fall on Ms. Clancy, who is held without bail." PATRICK CLANCY SPEAKS OUT AFTER HUNG JURY IN LINDSAY CLANCY CASE, ADDRESSES PROSPECT OF ANOTHER TRIAL In her appeal to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, Clancy's attorneys argued that Sullivan unnecessarily declared a mistrial and that forcing her to stand trial again would violate her constitutional protection against double jeopardy. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST The legal battle comes while another major change hovers over Clancy's case. Sullivan is preparing to retire in June 2027 when he reaches Massachusetts' mandatory judicial retirement age of 70. articles.title: OutKick's Do's and Do Not Do's to keep the Thanksgiving table conversations chugging along
articles.summary: Thanksgiving dinner conversation tips include wearing a pith helmet and debating "Grand Theft Auto VI," out for a week by the time the feast arrives.
articles.body: Thanksgiving is upon us. It's a day for food, football, and navigating a dinner with your extended family. That can be easier said than done, and one of the keys is keeping the conversation moving at the dinner table. Now, I have no problem sitting in silence around people. Of course, I'm also not (too much of) a psycho, and I understand that most people start crawling out of their skin when they can hear the blood flowing through their inner ear. So what is one to do? Well, I have some tips and tricks for what to do and what not to do to ensure that the Thanksgiving chatter keeps chugging along. Do: Choose your wardrobe carefully There's no rulebook for Thanksgiving attire, but it is one great way to have a built-in avenue for conversation. All you have to do is wear something that will lead to questions. Observe: * Chewing sounds are heard while you sit at the table wearing a nice collared shirt, khakis, and a pith helmet. "So, uh... so what's with the pith helmet?" End scene. Aaaaand we're off to the races. Now everyone is going to be chatting about their favorite pith helmet wearers, brands, and facts. This works for any piece of novelty clothing from propeller beanies to busy Hawaiian shirts to boutonnieres that spray seltzer in people's faces. Do Not Do: Make everyone go around the table and say what they're thankful for I appreciate the sentiment, but nobody likes doing this for a few reasons. For starters, nobody wants homework while they're trying to beat their personal record of stuffing servings. It also never leads to conversation. Everyone just nods and then moves on to the next sap. On top of that, all of the good things to be thankful for get used up early, which leaves those at the end scrambling. It never fails that by the time they get to you, the classics like friends, family, and health have been used several times. That means you've got to come up with something, and that usually winds up being "I'm thankful that the Lions covered" or "I'm thankful that I have off tomorrow because I'm on beer numero cuatro and it's barely one in the afternoon." Nothing wrong with being thankful for those things, but they will not make you look great. Do: Bring up 'Grand Theft Auto VI' "Grand Theft Auto VI" will have been out for a week by the time we sit down to stuff enough grub in our food holes to bring a proud tear to a pilgrim's eye. Considering it's already one of the top-grossing entertainment releases ever, everyone sitting at the table has played it, has thoughts on it, or has no clue what the hell it is. Sounds like conversation fodder to me. Maybe you start with how you robbed a thrift store and accidentally mowed down a lady on a Rascal scooter while making a break for it. Your uptight cousin might counter with how the game is proof of societal decay. Then your cool cousin could tell her to lighten up. After that, you can all spend the rest of the meal explaining to your grandma that it's a video game and you didn't actually flatten some biddy with a car you stole from a junkie. ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! Do Not Do: Bring up politics... unless you want to, in which case, go for it Traditionally, you steer clear of money, religion, and politics in mixed company. Talking politics is a great way to ensure that your cousin's pink-haired girlfriend with the Che Guevara shirt and permanent "I'm no fun" scowl on her face does not return the following year, but it could also cause some friction with folks you actually like. That's a shame because there was a time when people could have civil political discussions around the table. I think we should bring that back, but it needs to be done carefully. The trick is to read the room and ease into it. Start with something less polarizing and then work toward the stuff with teeth as you build up some goodwill. Do: Have a take on cranberry sauce I'm not sure why, but cranberry sauce is the black licorice of Thanksgiving food. Everyone either loves it or hates it. I love it (I love black licorice too; sorry for having a sophisticated palate), specifically my grandma's signature version with some Grand Marnier thrown in there, but I'll take the jellied kind too. WWE LEGEND 'STONE COLD' STEVE AUSTIN SHARES THANKSGIVING PLAN AND HOLIDAY STAPLE HE BELIEVES IS 'OVERRATED' Of course, some people will start dry heaving at the thought of a can of Ocean Spray and the ghostly visage of its former aluminum vessel baked into the side. It doesn't matter which side you're on; just have a take because this is one of the biggest points of discussion on Thanksgiving. It's up there with how you wouldn't be caught dead going out on Black Friday when you can shop online, and how your brother's ex-wife that no one likes has put on some pounds. Do Not Do: Critique the turkey that has been smoked to perfection for your ungrateful ass Here at stately Reigle Manor (my rented townhouse), we go the smoking route when it comes to turkey preparation. Some say frying is the way to go; others (perhaps incorrectly) throw it in a plastic bag sans seasoning at a randomly selected temperature and pray to the Butterball gods. What we don't need is a "CSI"-style forensic breakdown of the bird. "I think the white meat could've been a bit juicier." "The dark meat isn't quite as flavorful as last year." "This is dry and tastes like garbage." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! The only person permitted to give table-side critiques is the cook. Everyone else can save it for the post-game review on the car ride home. STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW! Now, my turkey always comes out immaculate, so this isn't an issue for me, but cut a bit of slack to the poor sap who rolled out of bed at 6 am to pull a turkey's own neck and a bag of its organs out of its abdomen (which is really messed up if you think about it) so that it was ready for showtime. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER The giant 15- to 20-pound bird you eat once a year wasn't to your liking? Well, then how about next year you violate the turkey while watching the crappy Broadway performances that we all hate but suffer through to see the Pikachu balloon? articles.title: US Army declares Iowa lead azide detonation ‘tremendously successful’
articles.summary: Army hails Iowa’s lead azide disposal operation as some experts warn of potentially hidden toxins.
articles.body:
United States Army officials have hailed Wednesday’s mission to destroy 68 drums of volatile lead azide — a sensitive munitions explosive — at a military base in Iowa as a success, saying it had “wildly exceeded their expectations”.

Speaking at a news conference in Middletown, a southeastern rural city adjacent to the ammunition plant where the operation was carried out, Major General Eric Shirley, the Army official in charge of the disposal effort, said overhead footage showed that “all of the lead azide barrels were definitively removed”.

The controlled detonation at 10:15am (16:15 GMT) destroyed approximately 4,500kg (10,000lb) of deteriorating lead azide — an explosive that has been used in military munitions since World War I.

“There was no secondary explosions. There was no kick-out. There was no infrastructure damage in or around our installation,” Shirley said, adding that the operation was “tremendously successful”.

Officials also said that extensive mitigation measures, including earthworks, foam barriers and gel blocks, had helped to absorb the shockwaves and toxic fallout.

However, Democratic Illinois House Representative Mike Quigley voiced dissatisfaction over how military leaders handled the operation, calling the holiday-eve scheduling and lack of communication “unconscionable”.

In a statement on X, the congressman wrote: “It is unfair that our military leaders are releasing 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide on our friends in Iowa the day before Thanksgiving.”

Following days of heightened alarm over lead dust contamination and its environmental repercussions, federal officials announced that preliminary data from Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) sensors had detected no airborne lead particles.

Ongoing monitoring efforts continue in the immediately affected blast zone.

A post on the agency’s social media account shortly after the operation said that “ALL EPA real-time air monitors are reporting ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region”.

Chemists have noted that lead, as a nonbiodegradable element, cannot be chemically decomposed or destroyed. It persists in the environment, with airborne particles capable of travelling considerable distances before settling on soil and potentially leaching into groundwater.

Detonating large stores of the unstable explosive would decompose the compound into its basic elements – nitrogen gas and metallic lead.

Lead is a potent neurotoxin that poses its sharpest threat to children and pregnant women, with links to learning disabilities, impaired neurological function, mental health challenges, reproductive harm, hearing loss and other impairments.

“The EPA can do millions of tests, but they [must also] test for the breakdown products and the stabilisers and plasticisers [containing] lead azide [which] are endocrine disruptors; some are cancer-causing chemicals,” said Scott Smith, an independent environmental testing expert who was heavily involved in air testing after the 2023 East Palestine, Ohio train derailment and industrial incidents.

The Army Sustainment Command said it would release a final breakdown of the affected area — including lead-dust dispersion and surface-deposition maps — after the operation.

“I believe absolutely that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanely possible the risk to the health and the safety of the people in Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Shirley.

articles.summary: Jean-Michel Basquiat's 1983 canvas Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads) sold for $32,880,000 at Christie's New York on Thursday, 19 November,
articles.body: Jean-Michel Basquiat's 1983 canvas Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads) sold for $32,880,000 at Christie's New York on Thursday, 19 November, becoming the top lot of the 21st Century Evening Sale at Rockefeller Centre. According to Christie's official press release, the sale of 56 lots totalled $145,863,200, selling 91% by lot and 92% by value. The release states that the Collection of Antonio Homem Sonnabend reached $41.9 million and the Collection of Agnes Gund totalled $25.7 million. Christie's also reports new auction records for Antonio Santín and Julia Jo. The running total for Christie's New York Marquee Week now stands at $852,190,776.Basquiat painting leads Christie's New York 21st Century Evening SaleThe 21st Century Evening Sale comprised 56 lots of art and design from the post-war and contemporary eras. The release says the sale totalled $145,863,200, selling 91% by lot and 92% by value. Christie's describes it as a strong sale.It followed a banner Wednesday that saw the highest-ever total for the Impressionist and Modern Art Day and Works on Paper Sales at Christie's New York. Christie's states that, combined with those results and the earlier Evening and Day sales, the running total for New York Marquee Week reached $852,190,776.Two collections were offered in the sale. It says the Collection of Antonio Homem Sonnabend exceeded expectations, reaching $41.9 million. Andy Warhol's Campbell's Soup Can (Turkey Noodle) sold for $9 million and Roy Lichtenstein's Large Spool for $8.6 million, with the proceeds of those two works intended to fund the Sonnabend Collection Foundation. Warhol's The Kiss (Bela Lugosi) sold for $4.6 million, and Lichtenstein's Small Wall Explosion sold for $800,000, over its high estimate. A Jean Prouvé "Centrale" ("Trapèze") table sold for $1.7 million after lively bidding took it well over its high estimate. According to Christie's, together with selections sold earlier this fall in New York, London and Paris, the Sonnabend collection has now realised $56.4 million.The Collection of Agnes Gund, sold to benefit the Gund Art Foundation, totalled $25.7 million. It was led by Vija Celmins's 1990 painting Untitled (Ocean), which Christie's says drew robust bidding in the room and on the phone and sold for $7.1 million. Robert Ryman's 1961 Untitled sold for $3.7 million, almost double its high estimate, after nearly five minutes of bidding. Jim Nutt's 1999 portrait Loom, which Gund once called her "Mona Lisa", sold for $1.1 million.Richter painting fetches $9.4 million as Christie's reports strong demandChristie's reports strong demand for a diverse group of contemporary works. A 1991 painting from Gerhard Richter's Abstraktes Bild series achieved $9.4 million. Joseph Yaeger's 2022 watercolour Intuition means to guard sold for $332,800, against a high estimate of $180,000. A 1982 photograph by Ana Mendieta sold to a client on the phone for $320,000 after competitive bidding.New auction records for two artists. A 2025 oil painting by Antonio Santín sold for $486,400. Julia Jo's large-scale abstract painting One Fell Swoop, the final lot of the night, sold for $409,600, more than thirteen times its low estimate. According to Christie's, the canvas was painted this year and was sold to benefit the Coalition for the Homeless. articles.title: A Washington home owned by US congresswoman Elise Stefanik’s family failed to sell at $1.99 million, then fetched $2.9 million in cash; city records now flag the transaction as unusual
articles.summary: A Washington home owned by US Congresswoman Elise Stefanik’s family sold for $2.9 million in cash months after leaving the market, even though it did not
articles.body: A Washington home owned by US Congresswoman Elise Stefanik’s family sold for $2.9 million in cash months after leaving the market, even though it did not sell at a lower asking price of $1.99 million. City tax officials have now marked the sale as unusual, saying the price was high compared with past listings and that some deal details could not be fully checked. The three-bedroom home on Independence Avenue SE sits about six blocks from the US Capitol and was sold in June to a new Delaware company called AFS Real Estate Holdings, whose backers are not publicly known. The Washington Post first looked into the sale, reporting on the price jump and the buyer's scarce public records, and in a follow-up story on 25 November reported that Washington, DC, property records gave the deal a special label called "Sale Code 4". That label has put new focus on the sale, which involved a home held by a company where Stefanik and her family members owned shares, while Stefanik’s office called the deal commercially reasonable and said it would appear in her required financial report.A property that failed to sellEMS DC Properties, a limited liability company tied to Stefanik and her family, bought the townhouse in August 2010 for a little more than $1.2 million, according to The Washington Post. Stefanik bought it with her parents and brother, and later reported an ownership stake in Washington residential rental property through EMS DC Properties. The home went on the market in September 2025 for $2.195 million, dropped to $1.99 million in November after failing to sell, and came off the market in February 2026 after more months with no buyer. The sale happened in June while the home was no longer listed for sale, changing hands for $2.9 million in all cash, which was $910,000 above its last asking price, with The Washington Post reporting that only two homes on Capitol Hill had public records showing a higher sale price over the prior year. The newspaper said it found no records or work permits showing renovations done in the four months between taking the home off the market and selling it, and records also showed no mortgage tied to the sale.Why the sale was flaggedThe D.C. Office of Tax and Revenue gave the deal "Sale Code 4", a label covering sales with unusual buyer-seller deals where the price does not seem to match market value. Office spokeswoman Brianna Jordan told The Washington Post that officials used the code because "the sale price was elevated relative to its prior listing prices, and the circumstances surrounding the transaction could not be fully verified." Jordan said off-market sales sometimes get this label depending on the facts of each deal, and the newspaper's check of city records found that under 500 property sales, or about 6 per cent of roughly 8,000 home and business sales recorded from January through October 2026, got Code 4, while most sales were logged as normal market-rate deals.Stefanik’s office pushed back on claims that the label was rare, initially saying about 6,000 property sales had been flagged as unusual that year. The Washington Post reported that number seemed to cover a much broader group of deals marked "unqualified", which uses many codes and does not mean every sale got Code 4, and after being asked to clarify, the office said 480 deals got a code similar to the one on the Stefanik home.Questions over the buyer and the priceThe buyer, AFS Real Estate Holdings, registered in Delaware roughly a month before the June sale, has no known online presence, and public record searches did not show who owns or runs it. Lawyer Janis M. Penman, a partner at the Washington office of Cleveland-based law firm BakerHostetler who filed the papers to set up the company, did not reply to a request for comment from The Washington Post. Stefanik did not answer written questions from the newspaper asking if she knew who owned or ran AFS, while her office said the home was listed during a government shutdown and "a slow holiday season", called the final sale a "commercially reasonable transaction", and said Stefanik held a minority share in the home. The office also said the price fit other historic townhouses nearby, stating: "The offer to buy the investment property was made and accepted within the range of prices for comparable historic townhouse sales in the neighborhood that range from $2-$4 million," according to its statement to the newspaper.The Washington Post asked six local estate agents and property lawyers with decades of Capitol Hill experience to review the sale, and none could recall another case where a buyer paid so much above a recent asking price. Settlement lawyer Patrick Tangney, who has 20 years of experience in the Washington area, said the price looked unusual based on listing and property records, while Capitol Hill estate agent Tom Faison, who has over 30 years of experience, told the newspaper: "A reasonable appraiser looking at six months of sales in my opinion would not be able to justify $2.9 million for this house," adding a question over whether buyers would overlook the home's recent failure to sell for less. The newspaper also reviewed 34 homes given by Stefanik’s office as examples of similar sales, finding that 13 sold for more than the family’s home, though most had more bedrooms or more living space, and some had features the Independence Avenue home lacked, such as a swimming pool, a garage or private parking. The townhouse itself was listed with three bedrooms, 3.5 bathrooms, three fireplaces and about 2,700 square feet of space.Family company bought a Virginia homeThe June 24 sale went through EMS DC Properties, the limited liability company in which Stefanik and her relatives held shares, and after selling the Washington townhouse, EMS bought a newly built home in McLean, Virginia, for $3.3 million. A paper tied to that purchase listed a $434,425 mortgage signed by Stefanik, who was named the company’s managing member. In a statement reported by The Washington Post, Stefanik’s office said she had shared required details in her yearly personal financial reports while in Congress, and added that the sale followed the law and House ethics rules and would go into her next yearly financial report. North Country Public Radio also covered the sale on 24 November, noting that the buyer's identity stayed unclear, the sale price was well above the last asking price, and the family bought the home in 2010 for about $1.2 million. articles.title: Maddow says Democrats can abolish Electoral College if they 'swing for the fences'
articles.summary: Rachel Maddow says abolishing the Electoral College is "doable" if Democrats swing for the fences after they won huge majorities in the 2026 midterms.
articles.body: MS NOW host Rachel Maddow said during an interview on Saturday that getting rid of the Electoral College was "doable" for Democrats if they "swing for the fences." MS NOW's Jacob Soboroff asked Maddow about her thoughts on Democrats getting rid of the system, which has received criticism after the last two Republican presidents won their first elections despite losing the national popular vote. "My whole life, it has been this kind of theoretical, you know, this hypothetical math problem. You know, if ever enough states to speak for 270 electoral votes all got into this agreement, then it would go into effect, and it always just seems so pie in the sky," she said. GOP WIPEOUT GOES FROM BAD TO WORSE AS DEMS QUIETLY SCORE ANOTHER MAJOR WIN WITH BIG RAMIFICATIONS Maddow said she felt it was doable for the Democrats after speaking with Ben Wikler, a Democratic advocate for eliminating the Electoral College. Soboroff and Maddow said that Democrats could use the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement that makes it so a state will award all of their electoral votes to whichever presidential candidate wins the overall national popular vote — regardless of who actually won the vote inside that individual state. GAVIN NEWSOM EXPRESSES 'OPENNESS' TO PACKING SCOTUS, CALLS ELECTORAL COLLEGE SYSTEM 'PERVERTED' Eighteen states have signed the compact, in addition to Washington, D.C., which means the compact has 222 electoral votes pledged to it — 48 short of the 270 needed to take effect. However, Democrats now control the governor’s office and both chambers of the state legislatures in the swing states of Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Nevada. Those legislatures' combined 50 electoral votes would push the compact to 272 and activate it should they vote to sign the compact. PROGRESSIVES UNVEIL $25 MINIMUM WAGE PUSH TO SOLVE AFFORDABILITY CRISIS DESPITE ECONOMIST INFLATION WARNING "There are enough Democratic states right now who have a Democratic trifecta — governor and the full legislature — that puts you way over 270 if they all decided to do it, and you don't need very many states to act right now for that to be operative," Maddow said. "It's doable. I mean, raising the minimum wage is doable. Getting rid of the Electoral College is doable, age limits for Supreme Court justices might be doable. I mean, the Democrats have big majorities and if they decide to swing for the fences, they could do a lot right now." KAMALA HARRIS CALLS TO EXPAND SUPREME COURT, ADD STATES IF DEMS TAKE CONGRESS Former Vice President and 2024 Democratic nominee Kamala Harris called for major institutional changes in October during an interview, which included "changing" the Electoral College. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "I believe that we need to expand the Supreme Court. We need more justices on the Supreme Court so that we can have a court that actually reinforces the spirit and principles behind the Constitution of the United States," Harris told podcast host Keke Palmer. "I believe that we should be pushing for what is possible around changing the Electoral College. Right?" she added. Harris also lost the popular vote in 2024, making her the first Democratic White House candidate to do so in 20 years. The system allocates 538 electors to the 50 states and Washington, D.C. A majority of 270 is needed to win the presidency. articles.title: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is pushed back to Saturday due to weather
articles.summary: Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Day parade will be pushed back to Saturday because of severe weather, officials said.
articles.body: Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Day parade will be pushed back to Saturday because of severe weather, officials said. “The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” Macy’s said Wednesday. The parade will now kick off at 8:30 a.m. ET Saturday. “Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday,” Macy’s said. The cancellation comes as the East Coast is forecast to be hit by stormy weather on Thanksgiving Day, bringing heavy rain, strong winds and coastal flooding, according to the National Weather Service. Since its debut in 1924, the parade has only been cancelled three times — in 1942, 1943 and 1944 — because materials for giant balloons were needed for the World War II effort. Balloons were last grounded in 1971 due to fierce winds and rain. City regulations mandate balloons can’t fly if sustained winds exceed 23 mph. New York officials will speak on the delay at 6 p.m. today. The historic parade, which marches from the Upper West Side to Macy’s Herald Square flagship store, is set to feature performers from nine Broadway shows, 100 balloons and inflatables, and a slate of beloved floats including Bugs Bunny, Curious George and Scooby-Doo. NBC said it will air last year’s Thanksgiving Day parade tomorrow at 8:30 a.m. in all time zones.
